info.name: 19 · Conversation tags & the tag schema
info.description:
Conversation **tags** and the per-evaluation tag schema that governs them: free-form key/value context an operator attaches to a conversation, which the backend folds into the model's system prompt.

**Flow.** A) the allow-list (`GET`/`POST`/`DELETE /evaluations/{id}/tag-keys`) — the admin tag schema, gated on `evaluations:update`; B) **free-form** tagging (`tags_restricted: false`) — any key is accepted; C) **restricted** tagging — only allowed keys, anything else refused; D) tagging **disabled** — every tag refused; E) removing a key retroactively narrows what reaches the model, without breaking the already-tagged conversation.

**Two independent flags, checked in this order.** `tags_enabled` decides whether tagging exists for the evaluation at all (off → the console renders no tagging surface and every tag is rejected). `tags_restricted` then decides *which* keys (off → free-form; on → the key must be in the allow-list, and an **empty allow-list while restricted forbids all tags**). Keeping "disabled" separate from "restricted with nothing allowed" is deliberate — otherwise the two are indistinguishable in the DB and neither the API nor the UI could tell a deliberate opt-out from a half-finished setup.

**Contract notes.**
- A refused tag is a **400** (`BadRequestError`), *not* a 422 — the payload is well-formed, it is the tag *policy* that rejects it. Two distinct messages: `Tagging is disabled for this evaluation.` and `Tag key(s) not allowed for this evaluation: <keys>.`
- `tags_enabled` defaults to **true** and `tags_restricted` to **false**, so a fresh evaluation is free-form — folder B asserts that starting state rather than assuming it.
- A duplicate key is a **409**; the allow-list is capped at `MAX_TAGS` (**16**) keys.
- Authoring and replaying are separate policies. Writes (`assert_tags_allowed`) **reject**; the fold into the prompt (`allowed_tags_only`) **drops** instead — so tightening the policy later must not leave an already-tagged conversation unable to send. Folder E asserts exactly that: after a key is removed, the stored tag survives on the conversation and the send still works.
- Tags live on the conversation (create + PATCH) **and** on a single message (`tags` on the send body), where the message layer overrides the conversation per key.

**Auth model.** Per-request. `{{admin_token}}` owns the schema and the conversations; `{{redteamer_token}}` proves a participant cannot edit the allow-list (`evaluations:update` is admin/owner only). Self-contained — creates and tears down its own model, group, evaluation and conversations. No manual token.

**Prereq.** `make seedlocal`.

Verified green on a live stack: 66/66 assertions (Newman).

request.description: Owns the evaluation, so it holds `evaluations:update` (the tag schema) and `conversations:*`.
A participant: holds `conversations:*` but **not** `evaluations:update` — the allow-list 403 in folder A.
No credential — this collection never needs a completion, only the write path.
`allowed_model_ids` must be non-empty and its members are the only models assignable to this group's evaluations.
A fresh group is `pending_approval`; evaluation creation 409s until it is approved (an owner may self-approve).

exec: pm.test('tagging is on by default', () => pm.expect(b.tags_enabled).to.eql(true));

request.description: The two flags are asserted at creation rather than assumed, so a changed default surfaces here instead of confusing folder B.
Body is `{model_id}`. The assign path re-checks the group's allowed-model subset — a model outside it is a 400.
Every conversation (group) targets exactly one scenario — the create posts to `/scenarios/{scenario_id}/...` — so the evaluation needs one before step 8.
A conversation needs a parent group. Its first conversation is the free-form subject in folder B.

exec: pm.test('the response is a bare array, not a page', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an('array'));

request.description: `evaluations:read`. Unlike most list endpoints this returns a **plain array**, not a `Page[T]` envelope — so there is no `items`/`total` to read and no `limit`/`offset` to pass. While `tags_restricted` is false these keys are inert.

exec: pm.test('echoes the key and its evaluation', () => { const b = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(b.key).to.eql('severity'); pm.expect(b.evaluation_id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('tg_eval_id')); });

request.description: `evaluations:update` — the tag schema is an admin/owner concern, not a participant's.
Two keys, so folder C can accept one and refuse another.
A partial-unique index among live rows is the arbiter, so a concurrent double-add loses cleanly rather than 500ing.

item.name: 5 · Keys are listed in key order

request.description: Ordered by `key`, so the console renders a stable list without sorting client-side.

item.name: 6 · A participant cannot edit the allow-list → 403

request.description: `red_teamer` holds `conversations:*` and can tag its own conversations, but the *schema* is `evaluations:update`. The permission gate runs before body validation, so this is a 403 and not a 422.

item.name: 1 · Tag a conversation with a key outside the allow-list

exec: pm.test('both keys stored, allow-list ignored', () => { pm.expect(t.anything).to.eql('goes'); pm.expect(t.severity).to.eql('high'); });

request.description: With `tags_restricted: false` the allow-list from folder A is **inert** — `anything` is not in it and is still accepted. This is the default state of every new evaluation.

exec: pm.test('tags land at create time too', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().tags.freeform).to.eql('yes'));

request.description: Tags are settable at create as well as on PATCH — the same `assert_tags_allowed` guard covers both write paths.

exec: pm.test('restricted now, still enabled', () => { const b = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(b.tags_restricted).to.eql(true); pm.expect(b.tags_enabled).to.eql(true); });

request.description: `evaluations:update`. From here the allow-list stops being decorative.

exec: pm.test('the earlier free-form key was replaced, not merged', () => pm.expect(t.freeform).to.eql(undefined));

request.description: The tag map is written as a whole, not merged key-by-key — the `freeform` key set in folder B is gone. Worth pinning: a client that PATCHes a partial map silently drops the rest.

exec: pm.test('a policy refusal, not a schema error', () => pm.expect(d.title).to.eql('Bad Request'));

request.description: **400, not 422** — the body is well-formed JSON of the right shape; it is the tag *policy* that refuses it. The message names only the disallowed keys, so a UI can highlight exactly those fields.

exec: pm.test('the smuggled key never landed', () => pm.expect(t.smuggled).to.eql(undefined));

request.description: A rejected tag map is rejected whole — the transaction rolls back, so no partial write.

item.name: 5 · A disallowed key on a *message* is refused too

exec: pm.test('the same policy guards the send path', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('smuggled'));

request.description: The send body carries its own `tags`, which override the conversation's per key — so the same guard has to run here. Refused **before** the turn opens, so no message is persisted and no SSE stream starts (`client_message_id` must be a UUID; a non-UUID is a 422). Step 6 is what proves the "nothing persisted" half.

item.name: 6 · …and no turn was persisted by it

exec: pm.test('the refused send left no message behind', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().total).to.eql(0));

request.description: The tag guard runs before `open_turn`, so a refused send is not a half-written turn: the transcript is still empty. Without this the previous step proved only the status code, while the description claimed the stronger guarantee.
The outer flag. The console renders no tagging surface for this evaluation at all.

item.name: 2 · Even an allowed key is refused → 400

exec: pm.test('the disabled message, not the allow-list one', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('Tagging is disabled'));

request.description: `tags_enabled` is checked **first**: `severity` is in the allow-list and still refused. The distinct message is what lets a UI say "tagging is off here" rather than "that key is not allowed".

exec: pm.test('the conversation keeps what it was tagged with', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().tags.severity).to.eql('critical'));

request.description: Disabling tagging stops *authoring*; it does not erase history. The stored map stays on the row — the fold into the prompt drops it instead (`allowed_tags_only`), which is what keeps an already-tagged conversation usable.

item.name: 4 · Sending still works with tagging off

exec: pm.test('the turn is accepted (SSE; the assistant errors without a credential)', () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.include('event:'));

request.description:
The reason authoring and folding are separate policies. This conversation holds tags an admin has since disallowed; if the *fold* rejected them, its owner could no longer send, regenerate or continue — over state the console now hides from them. Instead the tags are silently dropped from the prompt (and logged as `conversations.tags.dropped`).

⚠ SSE. Without a model credential the assistant turn finalizes to `error` while the user turn stays `complete`; the HTTP status is **200** either way.

item.name: E · Removing a key narrows the fold

exec: pm.test('enabled and restricted', () => { const b = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(b.tags_enabled).to.eql(true); pm.expect(b.tags_restricted).to.eql(true); });

request.description: Back to the state folder C ended in, so the removal below is the only variable.

item.name: 2 · Disallow the key the conversation is tagged with

request.description: `evaluations:update`. Soft-deletes the allow-list row. Note the key is addressed by its **name** in the path, not by the row id.

item.name: 3 · It is gone from the allow-list

request.description: A sibling removal leaves the rest of the schema alone.

exec: pm.test('says the key is not defined', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('severity'));

request.description: Idempotent in effect but explicit about it — a second delete is a 404, not a silent 204.

item.name: 5 · The conversation keeps the now-disallowed tag

exec: pm.test('history is not rewritten by a schema change', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().tags.severity).to.eql('critical'));

request.description: The stored map is untouched by the allow-list shrinking — an admin narrowing the schema does not mutate anyone's conversations.

item.name: 6 · And it can still be sent to

request.description: The payoff of the two-policy split: `severity` is no longer allowed, so it is dropped from the prompt — but the conversation is not bricked. Rejecting here would strand every conversation tagged before the change.

item.name: 7 · Re-writing that tag is now refused → 400

exec: pm.test('authoring is refused even though the stored copy survives', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('severity'));

request.description: The other half of the split: *replaying* the stored tag is fine, *authoring* it again is not. Same key, same conversation, different act — this pair is the whole design in two requests.

item.name: 1 · Delete the conversation group (cascades its conversations)

request.description: Children before parents.

item.name: 2 · Delete the evaluation (cascades the tag keys)

request.description: The remaining allow-list row goes with its evaluation.
The evaluation group leaks — groups have no DELETE route; `run_suffix` keeps its title unique.
